g.text: We use docker containers instead of jenkins tools in modern era because “In

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: production, Jenkins pipelines run builds inside Docker containers to ensure

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: consistency and portability. Jenkins itself only orchestrates the workflow.”

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When Jenkins runs a Docker container, the container is isolated and cannot

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: see the project source code present in the Jenkins workspace. This causes

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: the build to fail because tools like Maven or Node cannot find files such as

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: pom.xml or package.json. The -v (volume mount) option solves this by sharing a

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: folder from the Jenkins machine with the Docker container. Using -v

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: <host_path>:<container_path> mounts the Jenkins workspace inside the

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: container, allowing the container to read the source code and write build

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
